title: Correlation Is a Signal, Not a Cause
intro: Users who finished the onboarding tutorial had much higher three-month retention, so the team credited the tutorial. Maybe — or motivated users both finish tutorials and stay.

topics.title: Correlation Is a Signal, Not a Cause

learn.title: Same pattern, different stories
learn.text:
**What the team concluded:** tutorial → retention. So force the tutorial.

**What else could explain it:** motivated users do both.

Another example: “Learn more” clicks correlate with conversion, so add more buttons. Or: interested buyers click to read, and would have converted anyway.

try.q: Tutorial completers retain better. What is the competing explanation?
options: Motivated users both finish and stay
try.explain: Self-selection explains the pattern without the tutorial causing anything.

learn.title: Language discipline
learn.text:
Say **“is associated with”** or **“moves with”** — not “drives” or “causes”.

List the alternative explanations **before** presenting the pattern: self-selection, a third factor, or a reversed direction.

r runs from −1 to +1: close to ±1 the two move together, close to 0 they don't. The practical meaning matters more than the maths.

try.q: Which phrasing is appropriate for a correlation?
try.explain: Causal language overclaims what the data supports.

learn.title: Use it to design the next step
learn.text:
In real-world UX data, correlation is often all you have. Treat it as a reason to ask a sharper question — not as proof.

Next steps: an experiment, a staged rollout, or interviews with both groups.

**Regression** can show how much one variable predicts another while controlling for others — useful, but still not proof of cause.

try.q: What is the right response to an interesting correlation?
options: Design a study that can test it
Report it as a key finding
try.explain: An experiment, a staged rollout, or interviews with both groups.

options: There is no relationship of any kind
test.explain: It measures linear association, not all possible relationships.

test.q: When should alternative explanations be listed?
options: In the appendix of the report
test.explain: Self-selection, a third factor, a reversed direction.

options: How much one variable predicts another, controlling for others
test.explain: Useful, but still not proof of cause.

test.q: Why is correlation often all you have in UX?
test.explain: Which is why the discipline is in how you talk about it.

test.q: What is the risk of “so force the tutorial”?
options: You scale a cause that may not exist
test.explain: Acting on a correlation as if it were causal.
